1.sense: An oath opens the surah, and the thing sworn by is the Day itself. The particle before the verb is what the grammarians argue over: taken as a negative it denies something the deniers had been saying, taken as emphasis it makes the oath heavier rather than cancelling it. What is sworn to is never stated. The sentence breaks off after the second oath and comes back as a question.

notes.t: The la before uqsimu is read two ways. Some grammarians take it as extra, a sound that weights the oath, and read the line as a plain I swear. Others take it as a real negation of the denial just made, so the sense is not so, and I swear. The disagreement is old and neither side settles it from the wording alone.
notes.src: at-Tabari sets out both readings among the early grammarians

notes.t: The same formula opens three other oaths in the Qur'an, twice with a fa in front of it and once bare, so the construction is the Qur'an's own and not peculiar to this surah.
The word al-qiyamah occurs seventy times in the Qur'an and never once alone: it always follows yawm, the day of. This is the only surah that carries it as a name.

links.why: the objection the oath is aimed at, put in the deniers' own words: when we are dead and dust, that is a far return
the same denial with the bones named, in the surah that also asks when the hour is

2.sense: A second oath, and this time the thing sworn by is inside the person. An-nafs al-lawwamah is the self that turns on itself. The pattern of the word makes the blaming a habit rather than an occasion, something the soul does as a matter of course. A Day coming from outside and a conscience already at work within are set side by side.

notes.t: Lawwamah is the intensive pattern from l-w-m, to blame: not a soul that blamed itself once but one that keeps at it. The same pattern gives words for a person who does a thing constantly and by nature.
Two other states of the self are named in the Qur'an, the one that commands to evil and the one that has come to rest. Set with this verse they read as three conditions rather than three souls.

The exegetes differ over where the blaming happens. Some place it in this world, the believer taking himself to task for what he did and for what he left undone. Others place it on the Day of Rising, where every soul reproaches itself, the wrongdoer for his wrong and the doer of good for not doing more.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both, with reports for each

links.why: an oath by the self and by the proportioning that shaped it, the same witness sworn by from the other side
the whispering of a man's own self, known to the One nearer to him than his jugular vein

3.sense: The answer to the oath arrives as a question. The denial being answered is exact: not that Allah cannot act, but that scattered bones will never be brought back together. Jamaʿa, to gather, is the verb the surah keeps returning to. The objection is put in the mouth of al-insan, man as such, with no opponent named.

notes.t: A man brought a crumbling bone and asked who would give life to bones when they are decayed. That is the argument this verse reports, and the Qur'an answers it there by naming the One who made them the first time.
Allan is an with lan folded into it, and lan is the strong future negative. What is reported is not a doubt but a certainty in the other direction: never.
The root j-m-ʿ runs through the surah. It is refused here of the bones, done to the sun and moon in verse nine, and taken on as a promise about the Qur'an itself in verse seventeen.

links.why: the objection quoted in full: when we are bones and fragments, are we to be raised as a new creation
the answer the Prophet ﷺ is told to give to the man with the bone

4.sense: Bala answers a negative question by reversing it. The reply then goes past what was denied. Not the bones but the fingertips, the smallest and most particular work in the hand. Nusawwi is the verb of proportioning, setting a thing in its exact order, and it comes back at the end of the surah for the first making of man.

notes.t: The exegetes read the phrase two ways. One is that the fingers will be restored exactly as they were, joint by joint, so the fine work is easier than the coarse. The other is that the hand will be made flat and level, with no fingers to grip with at all, so the line is a threat rather than a reassurance.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both readings with reports for each

notes.t: Banan is the fingertips, or the fingers taken from their ends. The argument was about the largest and hardest parts of the body, and the answer names the finest.
The construction able to comes back in the last verse of this surah, and it carries the same argument elsewhere: the One who made the heavens and the earth is able to make the like of them.

links.why: the same verb of proportioning used of the first making, then balancing, then assembling in whatever form He willed

5.sense: Bal turns from the argument to the motive under it. The denial is not a conclusion he reached but a permission he wants: the road in front of him kept clear of any reckoning. Fajara is to break through a barrier that was holding something in. What he wants broken through is amamah, what lies ahead of him.

notes.t: The root f-j-r gives fajr, daybreak, which is light breaking through the edge of the night, and infijar, a bursting out. Fujur is a person breaking through the bounds set for him. The image is release, not weakness.

Amamah is read as the time in front of him, so the wish is to go on unchecked for as long as he has left; and as what is in front of him, meaning the Day of Rising itself, so the wish is to deny what is coming. The exegetes are divided and the word carries both.
notes.src: at-Tabari records both, and the two readings give different objects to the verb

notes.t: Fujur is named in the Qur'an as the counterpart of taqwa, the two put into the soul together, which is why it is a direction taken rather than an accident.

links.why: the same order of events, conduct first and denial after: none denies it but every transgressor deep in sin

6.sense: The question that follows the wish. Ayyana asks after a time held to be remote or unreal, and it is not the plain mata of ordinary asking. Nothing in the surah answers with a date. The reply is the scene itself, and it begins in the next verse.

notes.t: The same question is put twice more in the Qur'an, once by the deniers and once to the Prophet ﷺ directly, and neither time is a date given in reply.
The question is a challenge wearing the shape of a request for information. The surah treats it as such: it answers with what the Day looks like rather than when it falls.
Knowledge of the hour is kept with Allah alone, listed among the things no one else holds.

links.why: what the question will look like from the other side: as though they had stayed no more than an evening or its morning

7.sense: The scene opens on an eye that has lost its hold. Bariqa is what sight does when it is struck and can no longer fix on anything, the stare of someone past taking things in. Three short clauses follow, and in them the ordinary lights of the world go out one after another.

notes.t: The word is read two ways: bariqa, the eye confounded and unable to settle, and baraqa, the eye glittering and wide with fright. Both are transmitted readings and the exegetes carry both senses.
notes.src: at-Tabari sets out both; the difference is one vowel

notes.t: Eyes fixed open and staring are the Qur'an's regular picture of that day, once as the reason for the delay granted to wrongdoers and once as the moment the true promise draws near.

links.why: the same stare drawn out: heads thrust forward, the gaze not returning to them, their hearts empty air

8.sense: Khasafa is the verb for the moon losing its light, and it is also the verb for ground opening and swallowing what stands on it. The moon does not so much go out as go under. The light that measured the nights is taken first, and the sun follows in the next line.

notes.t: The same verb is used of the earth swallowing a man and his house, which is why the picture here is of a light sunk rather than extinguished.
The parallel scene puts the sun and the stars in the same two positions, wound up and fallen loose.

links.why: the moon split as a sign given in this world, before the moon is darkened in the next

9.sense: The two bodies that keep time apart are brought together. The whole order of the calendar rests on their never meeting: one rules the day, one the night, and months and years come out of the distance between them. Jumiʿa is the passive of the verb man refused in verse three. The gathering nobody thought possible is done to the sky first.

notes.t: Sun and moon run by an exact reckoning, and the sun is not free to overtake the moon. What is described here is that arrangement ending.
The verb jumiʿa is masculine although ash-shams, the sun, is feminine. The grammarians explain it by the pair being taken as one thing, the masculine carrying both.
The exegetes differ over what the joining is: the two darkened together, the two brought up from the same place, or the moon folded into the sun so that neither is told from the other.
notes.src: at-Tabari records more than one, with no report settling it

links.why: the sun wound up like a turban in the parallel scene

10.sense: The same al-insan who asked when the Day was now asks where to get out of it. Mafarr is the place of flight, the bolt-hole, and the question takes for granted that there is one somewhere. It is the last thing he is quoted as saying in the surah, and the answer takes one word.

notes.t: Mafarr is the noun of place from farra, to bolt, the way an animal breaks from a pen. What is being asked for is not escape in the abstract but somewhere to run to.
Flight was already answered in the Qur'an while it was still possible to try: fleeing will not benefit you if you flee from death or from being killed.

links.why: the criminals see the fire and find no way to turn aside from it

11.sense: One word of refusal, then the answer. A wazar is the high ground or the fastness people ran to when a raid came, cover that holds. The Arabs' own word for a place of safety is set against a day the mountains themselves do not outlast.

notes.t: The root w-z-r gives wizr, a load carried on the back, and wazir, the one who takes part of the load. Refuge and burden come out of the same three letters: the shelter is a thing that bears weight.
The same denial in other words: on the day you turn your backs in flight, you have no defender against Allah.
The mountains that a wazar is found in are themselves set moving and become a mirage.

12.sense: Where the flight ends. Mustaqarr is from qarra, to settle and stay, so it is the place a thing comes to rest rather than passes through. The runner arrives at the one place he was running from. The line is built to be said twice, and verse thirty says it again with a single word changed.

notes.t: The frame ila rabbika yawmaidhin holds both verse twelve and verse thirty, and only the last noun changes. Each ending rhymes with the passage it closes: the settling here, the driving there.
To your Lord is where the matter ends: the Qur'an says it of the hour and says it of everything.
The address turns for a moment to a single you, your Lord, inside a scene about man in general. The surah keeps this second person through to verse nineteen.

links.why: the same statement as a bare noun: to your Lord is the return

13.sense: The account is not read to him by a stranger. Yunabbaʾu is the passive of the verb for delivering news of weight, and what is delivered are the two ends of his record. Nothing is said here of a scale or a court. He is simply told, and the telling is the event.

notes.t: The same two verbs are paired in another surah of the same period, of a soul that knows what it sent ahead and what it kept back.
What a man sends ahead and what follows on behind him are both written down, so the record does not stop at his death.

The pair is read as his first deeds and his last; as what he did and what he neglected to do; and as the good he sent forward against the practices he left running after him. The exegetes carry all three and the wording admits them all.

links.why: the record that leaves out nothing small or large, and the finding of what was done set out present in front of them

14.sense: Bal turns again, from being told to already knowing. Basirah is sight that sees into a thing, and here the man is made the evidence rather than the one who gives it. He is a proof standing against himself. The feminine ending on a word describing a man is the Arabic way of making a quality total.

notes.t: The ta at the end of basirah is not gender but intensity, the same ending that turns a learned man into an allamah and a transmitter into a rawiyah. The man is not one who sees; he is sight itself, turned on himself.
Read your record, you are enough this day as a reckoner against yourself: the same idea with the book put into his hands.
Tongues, hands and feet give evidence against their owners, so the witness is drawn from the accused himself.

links.why: hearing, sight and skins testifying, and the man asking his own skin why it spoke against him

15.sense: The concession comes after the verdict, not before it. Alqa is to fling a thing down, so the excuses are thrown out rather than made, a man emptying his hands of everything he brought with him. What he knows about himself in the previous verse stands whatever he says.

notes.t: Maʿadhir is read as the plural of maʿdhirah, an excuse, and as the plural of miʿdhar, a screen or curtain hung to hide behind. On the second reading the verse is about a man drawing coverings over himself rather than speaking.
Excuses on that day are twice refused in the Qur'an: once as of no benefit to the wrongdoers, once as not even permitted to be spoken.

links.why: the shape the excuse takes when it comes: swearing by Allah that they had never been idolaters

16.sense: The scene of the Day breaks off and the address turns to the Prophet ﷺ while revelation is coming down on him. He had been repeating the words as they arrived, afraid of losing them, and the instruction is to let the tongue rest. The pronoun it is never explained. The surah is speaking about itself as it is being received.

notes.t: Ibn Abbas describes the Prophet ﷺ moving his lips with the revelation as it came, in the effort of holding it, and this verse being sent down about it. After that he would listen while it was recited and then recite it himself.
notes.src: Bukhari, Book of the Beginning of Revelation and Book of Tafsir on this surah, from Ibn Abbas

notes.t: The same instruction in other words: do not hurry with the Qur'an before its revealing to you is completed, and say, my Lord, increase me in knowledge.

Four verses, sixteen to nineteen, stand inside a passage about the Day of Rising, and the surah returns to that Day at verse twenty with no join. The interruption is part of the record: the revelation reports the conditions of its own arrival.

links.why: the Qur'an separated out so it could be recited to people at intervals, and sent down a sending down

17.sense: The reason the tongue can rest. The collecting of it is taken over by the One sending it, so nothing is lost by waiting. Jamʿ is the same word the bones were denied in verse three. One verb covers the gathering of scattered bones and the gathering of a scattered revelation.

notes.t: Quran here is a verbal noun, its reciting, and not yet the title of the Book. The next verse uses it the same way, so the word is caught at the moment it is becoming a name.
The undertaking is given again elsewhere in plain terms: We shall make you recite, and you will not forget.

links.why: why it came down in pieces rather than at once: to make the heart firm with it, and recited in a measured way

18.sense: The order of the two acts is set: listen first, repeat after. Qaraʾnahu puts the reciting on the side of the One who sent it, though the words reached the Prophet ﷺ through Jibril. What is asked for is following the recitation, keeping to what was said and to the way it was said.

notes.t: Ittabiʿ is the verb for walking behind someone, keeping his track. The tongue is put behind the revelation instead of racing alongside it.
The rule given to everyone else follows from the same principle: when the Qur'an is recited, listen to it and be silent.

When We have recited it is generally glossed as when Our messenger has recited it to you, since the words came through Jibril. Some read it as it stands, with the reciting attributed to Allah without an intermediary named.
notes.src: at-Tabari carries the first gloss from the early exegetes

links.why: how the recitation is to be given back: recite the Qur'an in a slow measured way

19.sense: Thumma puts the third undertaking after the first two, and after them in time. Bayan is making a thing plain. It is stated as a duty taken on, not a favour offered, so the Book is not left to be understood however anyone likes. What is explained is explained from the same side that sent it.

notes.t: Three things are taken on in three verses, each with the pronoun its and each with upon Us in front of it: its gathering, its recitation, its clarification. The sentence pattern is the argument.
The explaining continues through the one it was sent to: We sent down the reminder to you so that you may make clear to people what was sent down to them.
The exegetes divide bayan into the Book explaining itself and the explanation given through the Prophet ﷺ. Some restrict it to the first, holding that the verse promises only clarity in the wording.
notes.src: the difference is set out in the tafsir; at-Tabari carries the wider sense

links.why: the Book sent down so the Prophet ﷺ could make clear to them the very thing they differed over

20.sense: Kalla shuts the parenthesis and the surah returns to the Day, now with a plural you. Al-ʿajilah is the hurrying one, the life named for its speed rather than its size, with the word life itself left out. It is the same root as the hurry the Prophet ﷺ was told to leave off four verses earlier.

notes.t: Al-ʿajilah is an adjective standing where a noun was: the hastening one, with al-hayat, the life, dropped and only the feminine ending left to point at it. Al-akhirah in the next verse is built the same way, so the two halves match in grammar as well as in sense.
Nearly the same words are used of the deniers in the next surah: they love the fleeting one and leave behind them a heavy day.
Litaʿjala in verse sixteen and al-ʿajilah here come from one root, ʿ-j-l. One is haste with revelation and the other haste for what passes, and the surah puts them four lines apart.

links.why: what is granted to the one who wants the fleeting life, and what is prepared for him after it

21.sense: The other half of the sentence. Wadhara is to leave a thing lying where it is, not to argue against it. Nobody here is described as refuting the hereafter; they simply do not pick it up. Loving and leaving are given as one act with two faces.

notes.t: The verb wadhara is defective in Arabic: it is used in the present and the imperative and its past tense has fallen out of use, taraka filling the gap. What is left in the language is the ongoing leaving.
The same preference stated plainly, with the reason it is a bad exchange: you prefer the life of this world, and the hereafter is better and more lasting.

links.why: the man described by the same choice: he transgressed and preferred the life of this world

22.sense: The two ends of the judgment are drawn as faces, with nothing yet said about what anyone did. Nadirah is freshness, the look of a plant after rain and of skin that has come back to life. It is the first of a pair of words that differ by a single letter.

notes.t: The root n-d-r is bloom and freshness. Nazirah in the next verse is from n-z-r, looking. The two words are all but identical in sound, held apart by dad and za, and the surah sets them one line from each other.
The same radiance is given elsewhere as a gift handed to them, and elsewhere as something a viewer can recognise in their faces.

links.why: the same faces from another angle: bright that day, laughing, glad with news

23.sense: Where the radiance comes from. Nazara with the preposition ila is the Arabic for turning the eye onto something, and the thing named here is the Lord of those faces. In two short verses nothing else about the reward is mentioned at all.

notes.t: Jarir ibn Abdullah describes sitting with the Prophet ﷺ on a night of the full moon, and the Prophet ﷺ saying that they would see their Lord as they saw that moon, with no crowding and no difficulty in the seeing.
notes.src: Bukhari, Book of the Times of Prayer, and Muslim, Book of Mosques, from Jarir ibn Abdullah

notes.t: Most exegetes read nazirah as sight, since nazara with ila is the settled idiom for looking with the eye. Some read it from the same root as intizar, waiting, and take the sense as waiting for what their Lord gives. The difference is old and is argued from the grammar of the preposition.
notes.src: at-Tabari sets out both and holds by the first

notes.t: Those who do well have the best and something more besides. The exegetes who read this verse as sight take that something more to be the same thing.

links.why: the counterpart stated as a deprivation: they are veiled from their Lord that day

24.sense: The second group, drawn the same way and in the same number of words. Basirah is a face pulled tight and darkened, past frowning into something fixed. The parallel is exact: faces, that day, one adjective, and the sentence completed in the verse after.

notes.t: The same verb closes the account of the man in the previous surah who thought and measured and then frowned and scowled, so the expression here is one already given a history.
Basara is stronger than ʿabasa, the ordinary frown. Where the two are put together, the frowning comes first and this comes after it, as a face setting into what it has decided.
Faces on that day carrying dust and covered over with blackness, in the closing lines of another Meccan surah.

links.why: the same division by faces, whitened and blackened, with the reason for each stated

25.sense: Why the face is like that: not pain arriving but the certainty of it. Zann here is not doubt but settled expectation, the same use the surah makes of the word three verses later. Faqirah is named by what it does to a spine.

notes.t: F-q-r is the vertebra. A faqirah is a disaster that breaks the backbone, and faqir, the poor man, is one whose back has been broken by need. The calamity is named by the part of the body it goes through.
Zann carries certainty as well as guess, and the context decides: the criminals see the fire and are certain they are falling into it.
The verb is passive and no doer is named. Something is to be done to it, and the sentence leaves the hand that does it out of the picture.

links.why: the same faces given three lines instead of two: humbled, labouring, worn out, entering a blazing fire

26.sense: Kalla cuts the argument off and the surah drops into the last minutes of a life. The subject of reaches is not named: the soul is understood from the scene, exactly as it is left unnamed in the parallel verse about the throat. Taraqi are the collarbones, the stretch just below it.

notes.t: The parallel passage uses the same verb with the throat in place of the collarbones, and it too leaves the subject unspoken.
The feminine verb balaghat points to an-nafs or ar-ruh, both feminine, but neither is said. The omission is how the scene is drawn: everyone in the room knows what is meant.
The angels with their hands stretched out at the throes of death, in the one place the Qur'an describes the moment from outside the body.

links.why: the same bedside from the other side: We are nearer to him than you are, but you do not see

27.sense: A voice is quoted and not placed. Raq is from ruqyah, the words said over a sick man to lift what is on him, and the question is the one asked when everything else in the room has been tried. The same letters give the one who ascends, and the line has been read both ways.

notes.t: Raq is read as a healer, the question of the family standing round him, and as the one who takes him up, the question of the angels over which of them carries the soul. Both are carried in the tafsir and the wording does not decide between them.
In the transmission of Hafs there is a saktah here, a short stop taken without breaking the breath, between man and raq. The printed mushaf marks it with a small letter sin above the line.

links.why: the others in the room at that moment, described in three words: and you are looking on

28.sense: The dying man's own knowledge, given in the same verb used of the scowling face. Al-firaq carries the article: not a parting but the parting, the one every other separation was a rehearsal of. Nothing is said about what he sees, only about what he now knows.

notes.t: Zanna appears twice in this surah, at verse twenty-five and here, and in both places it is certainty rather than opinion. The word covers the whole range from guess to knowledge and the sentence around it decides which.
The same moment named from the other direction: the swoon of death comes with the truth, and the truth is what he had been turning away from.

links.why: the challenge put to the onlookers at that bedside: send it back, if you are truthful

29.sense: The body's own account of the moment. Iltaffa is used of things winding round one another, a vine on a trunk or a rope on a rope. What is described is one leg locked against the other, which is the last movement a body makes on its own.

notes.t: The exegetes read as-saq bis-saq as the dying man's legs twisting together in the struggle; as the last day of this world winding into the first of the next, one hardship joined onto another; and as the shrouding, when the legs are wrapped together. The wording is bare enough to hold all three.
The rhyme of this passage is a long a closed by qaf: raq, firaq, saq, masaq. The sound tightens as the scene does, four lines all ending on the same hard stop.

30.sense: The line from verse twelve comes back with its last word changed. Masaq is from sawq, the driving of animals from behind. The man who could not move his own legs is moved. Verse twelve ended at the place of settling; this ends at the journey there.

notes.t: Mustaqarr and masaq close the two halves of the surah, and the lines are identical except for the final noun. Each noun rhymes with its own passage, which is why the same statement is made twice in different words.
Both parties are driven, and the Qur'an uses one verb for it: the deniers driven to the fire in throngs and the godfearing driven to the garden in throngs.

links.why: the driving described with the word for bringing animals down to water: We drive the criminals to Hell, thirsty

31.sense: The verdict works backwards from the deathbed into the life. Two things are denied of him, one inward and one done with the body: he did not hold the message true and he did not pray. Saddaqa is also the verb behind sadaqah, so an Arab ear hears giving in it as well as believing.

notes.t: The people of the fire give the same account of themselves when they are asked what brought them there, and they begin with prayer.
Four verbs run across this verse and the next, two denied here and two affirmed there. The man is described entirely by what he did and did not do, and never by what he was called.
Saddaqa is read as holding the message true and as giving in charity. The exegetes carry both, and the word is wide enough that the pairing with prayer supports either.

links.why: a man who not only left prayer but stood over a servant of Allah to stop him praying

32.sense: The two acts that answer the two denials. Kadhdhaba is not simply to disbelieve but to call a thing a lie, an act done out loud. Tawalla is to turn the back and walk off. Together they are the Qur'an's standard pair for a man who has heard and has decided.

notes.t: The symmetry is exact: saddaqa against kadhdhaba, holding true against calling false, and salla against tawalla, turning to prayer against turning away. Two verses hold the whole man.
The same pair is used of the man who forbade another from praying, in a surah from the same period.

links.why: the same two verbs made into a description of the wretched one who will be kept from the fire's worst only by another's spending

33.sense: The last picture of him alive is a walk home. Yatamatta is the stretching of the back in walking, the gait of a man pleased with what he has just done. The fifth form makes it deliberate, something he does to himself. Nothing violent is described, only the ease of it.

notes.t: The word is traced to mata, the back, and also to madda, to stretch, with a letter changed. Either way the swagger is described as a lengthening of the body rather than as a speed.
The mockers in another surah are drawn making the same journey: when they turned back to their people, they turned back full of jokes.
The walk itself is addressed in the Qur'an as a thing that says something: do not walk in the earth exultantly.

links.why: the reason that walk is absurd: you will not tear the earth open nor reach the mountains in height

34.sense: A threat in an idiom that leaves half of itself unsaid. Awla is from waly, nearness, and the Arabs said it to a man who had just missed a disaster, to tell him how close it had come. Said four times across two verses with nothing named, it is menace without a noun in it.

notes.t: The grammarians differ over awla. Some take it as a noun, what is nearer, with the thing threatened left out. Some take it as a comparative, more fitting for you. Some treat the whole phrase as a fixed imprecation whose parts are no longer parsed. No reading is agreed.
notes.src: at-Tabari and the lexicographers record more than one derivation

notes.t: The phrase occurs in only one other place, of men who look at the Prophet ﷺ with the stare of someone fainting at death.

Many exegetes name Abu Jahl for the man described from verse thirty-one, and reports of an occasion for these words are carried in the tafsir. The surah names nobody, and the description fits a type rather than a person.
notes.src: the reports are recorded by the exegetes; the identification is not agreed

links.why: the same doubling of a threat in the previous surah: so may he be killed, how he measured, then may he be killed, how he measured

35.sense: The line is said again with thumma in front of it. The repetition is the whole content: nothing new is stated, and in Arabic threat-speech that is how a threat is pressed. Four occurrences of awla close the account of the man who walked home pleased with himself.

notes.t: Thumma here is not a step in time but a step in weight. The second saying is heavier than the first because it is the second, and the surah leaves the interval empty on purpose.
The device is used again in a later surah, where a warning is stated and then stated a second time with thumma in front of it and nothing added.

36.sense: The question of verse three comes back with a different object. There the denial was about bones, here it is about purpose: that a man might be let loose with nothing asked of him. Suda is said of a camel turned out with no herdsman, unmarked and unclaimed.

notes.t: A-yahsabu al-insanu opens verse three and opens this verse, and everything between them sits inside the frame. The two objections the surah answers are that the raising is impossible and that it is unnecessary.
The same question is put to a whole people: did you think We created you for nothing, and that you would not be returned to Us.
Suda carries no cruelty in it, only the absence of an owner's claim. The complaint being answered is not that man is treated harshly but that he is treated as though he belonged to no one.

links.why: the same argument widened to everything: We did not create the sky and the earth and what is between them in play

37.sense: The argument turns from what he will be to what he already was. A nutfah is the little water left in the bottom of a skin, a quantity too small to have a shape of its own. Yumna is poured out. He is asked to remember a state he cannot deny and had no hand in.

notes.t: Yaku is yakun with the final nun dropped, a lightening the Arabs allow with this verb when it is cut short. The shortest word in the line carries the man's whole past.
The drop is named at the start of two other accounts of the making of man, once as mingled and once as an extract of a fluid held in low regard.
The root m-n-y gives both maniyy and mana, to measure out and to appoint, the root behind maniyyah, an appointed death. Pouring and apportioning are carried by the same three letters.

links.why: the stages set out at length precisely as the answer to doubt about the raising

38.sense: The second stage, and then the making. ʿAlaqah is named for clinging: the root gives the leech and anything that hangs onto what it has fastened to. Sawwa, to proportion, is the verb of verse four, so what is promised for the fingertips is the same word as what was already done once.

notes.t: The stages are set out in order elsewhere, the drop made a clinging clot, then a lump, then bones, then the bones clothed in flesh.
The first words revealed to the Prophet ﷺ named man by this same stage: He created man from a clinging thing.

The fa in fa-khalaqa fa-sawwa is the fa of immediate sequence. Creating and proportioning follow with nothing set between them, which is the point being made against the man who thinks a second making is too much.

links.why: what follows the proportioning: the breathing of the spirit, and the giving of hearing, sight and hearts

39.sense: From one substance, two kinds. Zawj in Arabic is not the pair itself but one of a pair, each named by the other it belongs with, so the dual here counts two counterparts rather than one couple. Both are given as a single act of making, out of the same drop.

notes.t: Almost the same words appear in another surah, with the same pair, the same drop and the same verb of pouring, so this line is a settled formula rather than a fresh phrase.
Minhu is read as from it, the drop, and as from him, the man. The exegetes differ, and the sentence carries either without changing what it argues.
The article on adh-dhakara and al-untha makes them kinds rather than individuals: the male and the female as two classes drawn out of one material.

links.why: the same two kinds described as a gift assigned: He grants females to whom He wills and males to whom He wills

40.sense: The surah closes by pointing back over everything it has just described. Dhalika is the far demonstrative: the One who did all that, the drop, the clot, the shaping, the two kinds. Qadir answers the qadirina of verse four, and the question closes what the question in verse three opened.

notes.t: The same words end the same argument in another surah, with the answer written into the text: yes indeed, and He is able over everything.
The surah opens on la and ends on a question whose answer is bala, yes. Bala is also the first word of verse four, so the two halves of the surah are answered with one syllable.

It is reported that whoever recites this verse should answer it with bala, yes. The report is carried by Abu Dawud from Abu Hurayra and its chain has been criticised, so it is passed on as a practice with a disputed grading rather than as a settled sunnah.
notes.src: Abu Dawud, Book of Prayer, from Abu Hurayra; the grading is disputed

links.why: the reply given to the man holding the crumbling bone: the One who produced it the first time will give it life
